The card adds the degrees to 12, divides by 5 nodes, and gives the average degree 2.4." width="100%"} For directed graphs, this returns the average of (in-degree + out-degree). For undirected graphs, each edge contributes to the degree of both endpoints. In both cases the result equals `2 * edges / nodes`, since every edge adds one to the degree of each of its two endpoints. Average degree is a single-number summary of how densely connected a network is, which makes it handy for: - comparing the connectivity of networks of different sizes (unlike edge counts) - sanity-checking a generated or imported graph against an expected density - choosing parameters for random-graph models that should match a real network A single average can hide a lot: a five-node star and a five-node path both have an average degree of `1.6` but very different structures. Look at `degree_distribution()` for the full picture. Edge weights are ignored, parallel edges each count, and an empty graph gives `0.0`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Mean degree value across all nodes. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~aggregate_degree`) : Mean, median, and other degree summaries over chosen nodes. [](`~degree_distribution`) : How many nodes have each degree. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every node in a 4-cycle has two neighbors, so the average degree is `2.0`: ::: {#3995f1c8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec cycle = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A")] ) cycle.average_degree() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2.0 ``` ::: ::: The average is twice the number of edges over the number of nodes, since each edge adds one to the degree of both its ends. A five-node star has 4 edges, so its average degree is `2 * 4 / 5`, or `1.6`, though no node has that degree: the hub has `4` and the others `1`: ::: {#960966a0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph().add_star_graph(5).average_degree() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1.6 ``` ::: ::: ### The tightest circle In the Les Misérables network, characters are joined when they appear in the same chapter, and on average each character appears with 6.6 others. The nine students of the ABC society all appear with one another, so on their own they average 8, the most possible for 9 nodes: ::: {#35a75de3 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} novel = ec.les_miserables() students = [ "Enjolras", "Combeferre", "Prouvaire", "Feuilly", "Courfeyrac", "Bahorel", "Bossuet", "Joly", "Grantaire", ] society = novel.subgraph([novel.get_id_from_label(s) for s in students]) novel.average_degree(), society.average_degree() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (6.597402597402598, 8.0) ``` ::: ::: The society is highlighted in the novel. Its members meet each other and few others, apart from Gavroche, Marius, Mabeuf and MmeHucheloup, whose tavern they meet in: ::: {#f4463288 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} novel.plot( highlight_edges=society.get_edge_ids(), size_by="degree", show_labels=False, seed=1, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
